> **Generated — do not hand-edit this table.** Each row's source is
> `_registry/<DEF###>.row.md` (one file per defect); rebuild with
> `scripts/registers/gen_registers.py gen def`. See [How to add a defect](#how-to-add-a-defect).

The processed record of every **defect** — a thing that is broken or wrong versus the
spec. Two sources feed it:

- **User-reported** — filed in-app (`POST /v1/feedback/bug` → `bug_reports` table on
  melehost), triaged by [`/fix-bugs`](../../.claude/commands/fix-bugs.md). The DB is the
  intake queue; **this file is the processed record.** When a report is worked, it gets a
  `DEF###` here.
- **Prompt-reported** — a defect Saiful (or Claude) spots in a session with no in-app
  report behind it. No `bug_reports` row; still gets a `DEF###` here when processed.

Sibling register for *planned* change (new work, not fixes): [`../forward_planning/cr_list.md`](../forward_planning/cr_list.md).
Governance rationale: decision **D-058** in [`../initial_specs/11_decisions/decision_log.md`](../initial_specs/11_decisions/decision_log.md).

## How to add a defect

**This table is generated** — never edit it by hand. A shared monolithic table gets
*swept*: on the shared `main` checkout the second committer captures the whole index and
silently steals another track's uncommitted rows (the 2026-07-24 DEF095/096 incident —
[CR081](../forward_planning/CR081_registers_are_architect_write_only/CR081_registers_are_architect_write_only.md)).
One file per item removes the shared write entirely. Instead:

1. **The Architect mints the ID.** Ask for the next `DEF###` (zero-padded, sequential,
   never reused) — one minter avoids the ID-collision race. Pre-triage items use a
   topic-slug handle until the ID is assigned.
2. **The item's domain owner writes one row file** — `_registry/DEF###.row.md` containing
   that defect's single markdown table row (columns below). One file per item is a disjoint
   write-path, so two tracks never collide. **Source** is `bug:<short-id>` (first 8 chars of
   the `bug_reports.id` UUID) for user-reported, or `prompt` for prompt-reported.
3. **Regenerate + pathspec-commit:** `python scripts/registers/gen_registers.py gen def`,
   then `git commit -m "…" -- docs/defect/_registry/DEF###.row.md docs/defect/def_list.md`.
   Never bare `git commit` / `-am` / `git add -A` (those re-introduce the sweep).
4. Fix it on a branch; the fix commit carries `fix(bug:<short-id>): <summary> (AT:R<N> DEF###)`
   (user-reported) or `fix(<scope>): <summary> (AT:R<N> DEF###)` (prompt-reported). Update
   your row file's **Fix** hash + **Status** and regenerate.
5. For a defect needing its own root-cause / design write-up, create
   `docs/defect/DEF###_<snake_case_topic>/` and link it from the row.

**Status** mirrors the operational lifecycle: `resolved` · `wont_fix` · `closed` (fixed
out-of-band) · `open` (in the DB, not yet worked — not usually listed here until processed).

| DEF039 | 2026-07-09 | prompt | other | `reputation_events` has no DB partial-unique index on its `(user_id, event_type, ref_id)` dedup anchor — dedup is app-code-only (a SELECT-then-INSERT race), so concurrent same-ref awards can double-insert (defense-in-depth gap on a monetized currency). Fix: partial unique index (`WHERE ref_id IS NOT NULL`, since ref_id is nullable and award() only dedups when given one) on both the ORM model (`sqlite_where` too, for `create_all()`-backed tests) and migration 0015 for Postgres. `award()` now catches the resulting `IntegrityError` on the losing side of a race, rolls back, and returns 0 — same contract as the existing dedup-check hit. +1 regression test simulating the race (`test_reputation_service.py`). Migration verified via SQLAlchemy model load + the SQLite-parity test only — the Mac has no live Postgres to dry-run `alembic upgrade head` against (pre-existing repo constraint: the full chain already fails on SQLite at an earlier, unrelated Postgres-only migration); real verification happens at `/promote-to-alpha`. | resolved | — | AT:R54 |
| DEF040 | 2026-07-09 | prompt | other | Account merge mid-week re-keys `reputation_events` and sums lifetime `reputation` but does not recompute the adopter's current-week `league_members.points` — a mid-week claim can undercount current-week league standing (lifetime reputation stays correct). (CR004 audit round-1 finding F5) Root cause: the league-seat re-key (`_rekey_skipping_conflicts` on `LeagueMemberRow`, conflict_col=week) drops the orphan's seat outright whenever both sides already hold one for the current week — the common case — leaving the adopter's `points` frozen at its pre-merge value even though the orphan's `reputation_events` (re-keyed just above it) now belong to the adopter. Fix: after the reputation re-key, if the adopter holds a current-week seat, recompute its `points` as a full resync (`sum(reputation_events.points)` over the current ISO week's bounds via `league_service.week_end()`) rather than a delta — correct regardless of which side's seat survived. +1 regression test that fails at `3 == 11` without the fix. | resolved | — | AT:R54 |

| DEF049 | 2026-07-11 | prompt | other | Streak-milestone **credit double-grant under concurrency** (monetized currency). `reputation_service._grant_milestone` calls `award(…, always_record=True)` then grants credits (`user.credit_balance += credits` + `SubscriptionEventRow`) **unconditionally**, without checking whether *its* `award()` call actually wrote the guard row. After DEF039 added the partial-unique index + `IntegrityError`→rollback→return-0 to `award()`, the loser of a concurrent same-milestone race rolls its guard-row insert back yet **still grants credits** → a one-time double credit. Surfaced by the DEF039 audit (finding O1); pre-existing and orthogonal (before DEF039 the same double-credit occurred *plus* a duplicate guard row, so DEF039 is neutral-to-positive here — not a regression). **Naive gate on `award()>0` is wrong** — a legitimately cap-clipped milestone returns 0 with the guard row written and credits owed (the exact F1 case `always_record` exists for). Fix: opt-in `_raise_on_race` flag on `award()` — the milestone path passes it, so a race-loss raises instead of returning 0, and `_grant_milestone` skips the credit grant; all other callers keep the return-0 contract. +1 regression test. Agents default to reading it as a per-trade stop-distance budget, which makes any name with a wide technical stop un-buyable regardless of sizing. This is not the safety floor working as designed — the floor is a portfolio constraint, and the Room is applying it as a position constraint. Suspected material contributor to the benchmark's 24% approve rate vs the Street's 63% buy rate. | DEF110 | 2026-07-26 | prompt | sim | **Stop/target hit marks a sim trade won/lost + stamps realised P&L but never closes the position — the holding persists as phantom shares.** `SimEngine.evaluate_outcomes` (backend/app/services/sim_engine.py) flips a stop/target-hit BUY to `won`/`lost` and sets `realised_pnl = (price − entry) × qty`, but — unlike `manual_close`, which calls `_apply_sell_row` (reduce holding + credit cash) — it does **not** touch `sim_holdings` or `current_cash`. So after a target/stop hit the user still "holds" the shares: they can sell the same position again (double-realise P&L), and `total_value`/`drawdown_pct` are inflated by the phantom position. That account's trade ledger is 1 open · 1 won · 5 lost · 2 closed — **the 2 manual closes liquidated correctly and all 6 auto-outcomes did not**, which is the asymmetry this defect names, measured rather than inferred. `abc5e232` holds TSLA 3 of which 1 is phantom (partial); `821d7ced` holds IBM 1, fully phantom. **The severity line above is now WRONG and is corrected here: this DOES reach the safety floor.** CR026 wired the sector-concentration cap after this defect was filed, and it reads the same `sim_holdings`: `_build_room_sector_context` (`room_runner.py:729`) → `allocate_by_sector` → `check_mandate_compliance(holdings=…)` → a sector breach is a hard `REJECT` with `overridden_from_llm=True`. Computed for `8f1e288a` at cost basis with the production sector snapshot (AMD/HPQ/INTC = `Technology`; RXT/SPCX/SCHD unclassified): **the app shows Technology at 75.4% of a $7,928 portfolio and flags a breach of the 40% cap, when the real portfolio is one $197 SCHD position with zero Technology exposure and no known-sector weight at all.** So a Technology BUY in that user's Room is vetoed by the safety floor on a concentration made entirely of shares they do not own — a confident, mandate-shaped refusal derived from stale state, which is the DEF059 class. **97.5% of that account's displayed invested value is phantom.** This also inflates `total_value` and `drawdown_pct` everywhere they are read. Fix scope (a)+(b) in the original filing is unchanged and still correct; what changes is priority — this is not a display nit, it is corrupted input to mandate enforcement, and it needs a **backfill** for the three affected accounts as well as the code fix, since the stale rows are already written.  **CODE FIXED (AT:R65, 2026-07-29) — status stays `open` until it is promoted AND the backfill has run on Alpha, because the live corruption is still there until both happen.** (a) `evaluate_outcomes` now loads the portfolio row **once before the loop** and calls `_apply_sell_row` on every hit, so a stop/target close reduces the holding and credits the proceeds exactly as `manual_close` does. `_apply_sell_row` gained two guards the loop makes reachable: it skips holdings already `s.deleted` earlier in the same pass, and it clamps the sale to the shares actually on the books, crediting cash only for what it sold — without either, N trades closing against one holding pay the user for shares that no longer exist. It is a **state repair, not a replay**: phantom = `held − (Σ open buys − Σ open sells)`, the same fully-closed rule `cost_basis_lots.py` applies, so it is idempotent — the naive "credit every won/lost trade" shape double-credits on a second run, which on a money column is the worse failure. | DEF119 | 2026-07-27 | backend | api | **`freeze()`'s 2-per-year streak-freeze cap is an unprotected COUNT-then-INSERT — two concurrent requests can both pass the check.** Found by the CR091-STREAKS auditor (track U, independent) as its single MINOR finding; the lane was still voted **COMPLETE round 1** because the blast radius is narrow. `reputation_service.freeze()` enforces the Floor Manager perk's 2/year cap with a `SELECT COUNT(*)` immediately followed by an `INSERT`, with **no `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and no constraint spanning "count of rows per user per year."** The only DB constraint is `UniqueConstraint(user_id, frozen_date)` on `StreakFreezeRow`, which prevents re-freezing the *same* date and does nothing for two *different* dates requested concurrently. **The auditor's reproduction was inconclusive and says so:** it seeded one legitimate freeze, opened two uncommitted sessions and called `freeze()` on each for different new dates — both calls got past the stale COUNT before either committed (so the race window is real at the code level), but SQLite's coarse file-level write lock threw `database is locked` on the second insert. That lock is an artifact of the **test engine**, not the application; Postgres's default READ COMMITTED — the actual production engine — does not serialise this. Evidence is therefore structurally reasoned, not mutation-confirmed, and cannot be settled without a live Postgres instance (unavailable: the Mac is a pure editor). Worst case is a paid-tier user obtaining a few extra streak-freeze days per calendar year — **no credits, no money, no security/safety/compliance surface** — which is why this is MINOR rather than a blocker on the lane. Recommended fix: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the count query, or an equivalent serialising constraint. Note the cap's period is the **calendar year** (`period_key = str(target_date.year)`), confirmed from code during the audit. Fix shape: give the trailing test an explicit `else`/`true`, or end `print_state` with an explicit `return 0`, and — because the whole point is that nobody noticed — pin it with a check that asserts both watchers exit 0 on a populated `state` read, rather than only fixing the one line. The failure is the **silent-fallback** class this project degrades loudly against (CR040): a dead watcher and an empty queue are byte-identical from the outside, so the auditor's checkpoint memo recorded "queue is EMPTY" — true at 00:11, wrong by 02:07 — and every subsequent report inherited it. Do **not** fix it by making the watcher more robust alone — that reduces the frequency without restoring the signal, and this project's rule is that anything gated on a process being alive must fail visibly, never silently. Note the sibling constraint from **DEF132**: `watcher.sh state` currently exits **1** on a successful read, so any liveness check that gates on its exit code inherits an inverted signal and must be built after (or alongside) that fix. NO <ROLE> WATCHER` line and `dispatch.sh inbox` exits 1 on it, putting the signal on the Architect's per-work-unit gate. **Absence is deliberately NOT an alarm**: an auditor spawned per item is told not to watch, so no-heartbeat is normal under that model and alarming on it would be permanently red — the CR099 alarm-fatigue rule. **TERM and KILL are deliberately not trapped**: a teardown-killed watcher is exactly the failure being caught, and cleaning up on the way out would erase the evidence; INT is trapped because a human pressing ctrl-C already knows. Staleness = 3 missed polls, floored at 90s against scheduling jitter. Pinned by `backend/tests/unit/test_orchestration_watcher_contract.py`, including the check the row asked for — **start a real watcher, SIGKILL it, assert the board says so** — plus both no-false-alarm directions (clean exit and `-t` timeout each clear the stamp; absent and fresh stamps stay silent). Mutation-proved: removing the heartbeat writes turns the kill-mid-run pin RED; removing the `inbox` gate turns the inbox pin RED. The W3C server-sent-events line-splitting rule terminates a line on **CRLF, LF, *or* a lone CR** — so a bare `\r` inside a `data:` field ends that field for a compliant reader, and `\r\r` produces the blank line that ends the *event*. Rejecting is the stronger read: no producer has a legitimate reason to put a carriage return in streamed prose, and a raised error surfaces at the source instead of corrupting a transcript. Either way the whole-tree invariant in `test_def127_sse_framing_invariant.py` extends to cover it, and the escape decision gets a comment saying *why* the two framers differ. Note the breach copy already said *"of your portfolio"* while the arithmetic used invested value alone: the words and the maths disagreed, which is the CR046 shown-equals-enforced rule. **Two distinct defects in the same three lines, pointing in opposite directions.** **(A)** `sector_cap_breach` divided by `sum(current.values()) + proposed_value`. The correct denominator is total portfolio value **pre-trade** — a BUY spends cash to acquire shares, moving value between two buckets and leaving the sum unchanged, so adding `proposed_value` double-counted the purchase and put the cap in the wrong place even for funded portfolios. `portfolio_value` was *already* passed into `check_mandate_compliance` by both callers (`sim_engine.submit` sends `self.total_value(user_id)` = cash + holdings) — the sector check simply ignored it. It is now a **required** keyword, not a defaulted one, so a caller that cannot supply it fails loudly rather than silently falling back to the arithmetic that caused this. **(B)** `proposed_value` was priced off `limit_price` alone, which is `None` on a MARKET order, so it computed `0.0` and the check returned `None` at its first guard — **the sector cap never fired on a market buy at all.** A hole in the safety floor in the opposite direction, hidden because the same code that over-blocked new users under-blocked everyone else. Fixed by falling back to the mark already present in `quotes`; `sim_engine` now also prices the *proposed* ticker, since both call sites previously sent only held tickers and a first-time buy of a new name therefore had no quote to fall back to. **Display half — shown must equal enforced.** `allocate_by_sector` gained a `cash` parameter and a `CASH` bucket, and `NON_SECTOR_BUCKETS` excludes both `Cash` and `Other` from the concentration judgement. The bucket is required, not cosmetic: `_DonutPainter` re-normalises whatever it is handed (`sweep = value / sum(values)`), so returning weights that merely summed to <1 would have been silently redrawn as invested-only proportions and the donut would keep showing Technology 100% while the floor allowed the trade. `api/portfolio.py` passes cash and reports `total_value` as cash + invested; `room_runner._build_room_sector_context` passes it too, so the weights the twelve agents reason from are the same ones the floor enforces and the donut draws. The fourth, `test_room_runner_live_pm_enforce_safety_floor_rejects_sector_breach`, only ever went red because `run()`'s **placeholder $20,000 `portfolio_value`** was judging a real $10,000 book: the PM's requested 20% size is clamped to `risk_tier_cap(risk_score=3)` = **3%** before it reaches the floor, so on a consistent book the approved position is $300 and a sector already at 30% lands at 33% — under the cap, no veto, and the test's premise evaporates. Tap to retry.` **Root cause, exact.** [`ticker_chart.dart:29`](../../../mobile/lib/widgets/ticker_chart.dart#L29) declares `const List<String> _kPeriods = ['1D', '1W', '1M', '3M', '1Y', '5Y']` and passes the selected label verbatim through `tickerHistoryProvider` → `api.simHistory(ticker, period)` → `GET /v1/sim/history/{ticker}?period=1M`. The backend answers `{"detail":"invalid period; must be one of 1d,1w,1m,3m,1y,5y"}` — **lowercase only**. **Measured against live Alpha, not inferred:** all 6 periods × 3 tickers (TDG, NVDA, AAPL) = **18/18 HTTP 422**. Omit the parameter entirely and the same endpoint returns a full candle series (`"period":"1m","source":"yfinance"`, real OHLCV) — so market data, yfinance, the cache and the serialiser are all healthy. **The only fault is letter case, and it takes out the entire feature.** **Why nobody caught it, which is the more important half.** The failure degrades to `Chart unavailable. Tap to retry.` — copy that describes a *transient* fault. A user reads it as a network blip and taps retry, which re-issues the identical malformed request and fails identically, forever. There is no state in which that button can succeed. So the feature has been 100% dark on Alpha with **zero bug reports** until Saiful happened to ask why the chart was missing — a silent total outage wearing the costume of a flaky network, which is precisely the question CR040 tells us to ask (*if this fires constantly and silently, what does the user end up believing?*) and the answer here is: that their connection is bad. **Fix shape:** normalise the case (client-side `.toLowerCase()` at the call site is the one-line version; normalising server-side additionally repairs the **already-shipped `+56`/`+57` builds in testers' hands without an app update**, which is worth weighing since TestFlight users cannot be fixed by a client-only change until the next build). **The guard is the part that matters** and must ship with it: a test asserting every entry in `_kPeriods` is accepted by the server's allow-list, so the two lists cannot drift again — this is a contract between two files in two languages with nothing tying them together, which is `failure_patterns.md`'s recurring shape. A second, cheaper guard worth considering: make the retry surface distinguish "request rejected" (4xx — never retryable) from "network failed" (retryable), so a permanently-broken call can never again present as a transient one. **RULED (Saiful, 2026-07-29 0900 check-in): "File it and lane it"** — offered a fix-in-session given the one-line diff and the total outage; he chose standard track-R handling. Lane with the mobile batch. Relates to **CR040** (degrade loudly — the retry copy is the violation), **DEF073** (the adjacent class: error surfaces that misdescribe what happened). **RULING SUPERSEDED (Saiful, 2026-07-29, later the same day): fixed in session, server-side first.** The 0900 "file it and lane it" was made before the *server-side* half was weighed. Asked how soon a build could reach testers, the answer was that a build would carry almost nothing — one mobile commit exists since `+57` — while this, the largest live breakage, needs no build at all: **normalising on the server repairs the `+56`/`+57` binaries already installed**, and laning it with the mobile batch would have left the chart dark on every device until the next release. `sim.py` now lowercases and strips the token before the allow-list check and **echoes the canonical form it actually served**, not the caller's spelling — the client keys its 60s cache and its chip selection off that field, and CR046's shown-equals-enforced rule applies to a period the same as to a number. Normalising *spelling* is explicitly not normalising *meaning*: `bogus`, `1month`, `1 m` and empty are still 422, pinned by test. `api_client.dart` lowercases at the call site too, but as the belt to the server's braces — the chip labels stay uppercase because they are UI copy, and a client-only fix reaches nobody already installed. **The guard the row demanded is built and is a genuine cross-language contract test**: it reads the `_kPeriods` declaration out of `ticker_chart.dart` and asserts every label normalises into `VALID_PERIODS`, so the two lists cannot drift again — plus a vacuity guard asserting the chips are still declared uppercase (lowercase them and the contract test would pass while proving nothing) and a server-only pin of the six canonical tokens that runs where `mobile/` is not checked out. **11 tests; three mutations independently RED** — revert the server normalisation (7 RED), lowercase the Dart chips (vacuity guard RED), add a 7th chip with no server period (contract test RED). Backend **1567**, mobile 210, `flutter analyze` exit 0. **Deliberately NOT done here:** the row's second suggested guard — making the retry surface distinguish a 4xx (never retryable) from a network failure — is a client UX change and belongs to the mobile batch with DEF148/DEF150; the misleading *"Tap to retry"* copy is still misleading for any other 4xx. **FOLLOW-UP SCOPED, NOT YET BUILT (AT:R65, 2026-07-29) — and there are THREE states collapsed into one, not the two this row named.** `ticker_chart.dart:97-106` renders `_ChartError(label: l.tickerDetailChartUnavailable)` — *"Chart unavailable. Tap to retry."* — from two different branches of the same `AsyncValue.when`, and the `error: (_, __)` callback **discards the error object entirely**, so the plumbing to tell them apart does not exist yet either. The three: **(1) transient** — network down, timeout, 5xx: retry is the correct instruction and the copy is right. **(2) A 4xx** — the case this row already identified: retrying re-sends an identical request and gets an identical rejection, so the copy promises a remedy that cannot work. **(3) `data:` with `history.candles.isEmpty` (`:103`) — the request SUCCEEDED.** This is not an error at all; the server answered, with no candles. A ticker with genuinely no history for the selected period (a recent listing on `5Y`) hits this on every visit and can never clear it. **Shape of the fix:** branch on the error rather than discarding it — `friendlyError()` (built for **DEF148**) already distinguishes 4xx/5xx/timeout/connection and is the right vocabulary — and give state (3) its own non-error empty state with **no retry affordance**, since a tap that cannot change the outcome is the same broken promise in a quieter register (**CR040**: if this fires constantly and silently, what does the user end up believing?). **Deliberately deferred, and the reason is recorded rather than left implicit:** all three states need **new user-facing copy**, so new ARB ids in all three files — and the live **CR120** lane is holding `app_en/ar/ms.arb` to append 21 keys. The eighth is the non-vacuity check that matters most here: it renders all three states in turn and asserts they produce **three distinct strings**, so a future edit collapsing any two of them fails even though each individual test would still find its own text somewhere on screen. **Mutations measured:** making every error retryable again → **3 RED**; routing the empty-success case back through the error copy → **2 RED**. The *single-name* cap immediately above it, step 6, was left on the old formula — `(proposed.limit_price or 0.0) * proposed.quantity` — which is `0` for a market order, and the `proposed_value > 0` guard then skipped the check entirely. **Measured through `check_mandate_compliance` with no sector context, so only step 6 could fire:** `limit` $9,000 of a $10,000 book (90%) → blocked, *"position size 90.0% exceeds single-name cap 50.0%"*; `market`, same $9,000, same book → **passed, zero violations.** Identical economics, opposite ruling, decided by an order-type field a concentration cap has no business reading — and the app's trade ticket submits market orders, so this is the path a user actually takes. The floor still overrides an APPROVE with `overridden_from_llm=True`, so the effect is one-directional: the cap could only ever fail open. **Same defect, same three-line neighbourhood, same morning — and DEF149's own fix walked past it.** That is the finding worth keeping. The two caps each priced the proposal *for themselves* off the same source, so they were two renderers of one rule with neither a superset (the **DEF098** shape); fixing one and missing its twin was not an oversight the fix could have caught, it was the shape making the miss invisible. The repair is therefore structural rather than a second `or`: **the proposal is now priced ONCE, at step 6, and both concentration caps read that one number** — they can no longer disagree about what the trade is worth, so the next pricing change cannot reach one site and miss the other. **CR040, the unevaluated case:** a buy with neither a limit price nor a quote still passes both size caps — there is nothing to compare against, and inventing a ruling would be the DEF059 inversion — but it now emits `safety_floor_proposal_unpriced` with the ticker, order type and whether a quote was present. Its premise is in fact unsatisfiable in one buy: the cap is measured against total portfolio value, so while cash is still the larger share of the book, any notional exceeding cash is over the cap by construction. It now takes two buys to drive cash below half, and the premise is **asserted** rather than described. `test_mandate_audit.py::test_audit_endpoint_surfaces_violation_after_blocklist_patch` carried the comment *"Buy something — under 50% single-name cap"* above a fixed `quantity=20`, which at the walked mark was **77.1%**; it is now sized against the live price. | DEF157 | 2026-07-29 | prompt | mobile | **A release can ship one store and silently skip the other — `+57` went to TestFlight and never went to Play at all, and nothing anywhere noticed for a week.** Surfaced by Saiful 2026-07-29 as *"we have a drift in the build number for IOS and Android. they should both be 58. android is showing 56"* — reported as a drift in the artifacts, but **measured, the artifacts are not drifted**: `pubspec.yaml` and `android/local.properties` both read `0.1.0+58`, the built APK carries `versionCode 58` (read out of the binary manifest), the AAB is the same build, the melehost tester rig's APK is **byte-identical to the local one by sha256**, TestFlight has `58`, and `google_play_track_version_codes` reports **`internal → [58]`**. The `56` is what was **installed on the device** — Play had not yet propagated the release uploaded minutes earlier. **The real defect is why the gap is TWO builds instead of one:** `+57` was built and uploaded to TestFlight on 2026-07-28 and **was never published to Play**, so Android's last delivered build stayed at `56` while iOS moved to `57` and then `58`. **Mechanism — two independent bump paths with no parity check.** `scripts/build_testflight.sh` and `scripts/build_playstore.sh` each own a `DO_BUMP=1` and each bumps `pubspec.yaml` themselves (`build_testflight.sh:47,86`, `build_playstore.sh:55,87`). Running one without the other advances the shared version for **both** platforms while shipping only one, and nothing in either script, in the promotion protocol, or in any test compares what the two stores actually carry. This is the **P11 shape** — one rule ("both stores ship the same build number") implemented in two places with nothing tying them together — and the **CR040 shape** on top of it: the failure is completely silent, so the only signal is a human noticing a number in the app days later, which is exactly what happened. **Consequence beyond the number:** every Android tester was two builds behind for a week, so any bug report from an Android device in that window was filed against code that was not the code we thought was running — which corrupts triage, not just tidiness. **Second observation from the same measurement, and it is INERT — the first version of this row overstated it and is corrected here.** The Play **closed testing track** (API name `alpha`) holds `versionCode 43` under a release named `ami_trade_release`, against internal's `58`. I initially recorded that as fifteen builds of live staleness and warned that any tester enrolled in closed testing had been running a weeks-old build. **That was wrong, and querying the Play Developer API directly rather than only `google_play_track_version_codes` is what showed it: the release's `status` is `draft`, not `completed`.** A draft release is never served to anyone, whatever the enrolment. So nothing is stale in the field and no tester is stranded — it is an abandoned half-finished release, created around 2026-07-21 when `+43` was current, and left in the console. Consistent with `mobile/android/fastlane/Fastfile`, which has only ever targeted `track: "internal"` (CR048) — our automation has never written to the closed track, so this is a manual console leftover. `beta` and `production` are empty. **Disposition: cosmetic cleanup, not a defect** — discard the draft in the Play Console or leave it; it changes nothing either way. Recorded rather than deleted because the *method* matters: a track-version query alone reports a version code with no indication of whether it is live, which is precisely the kind of number that reads as alarming and is not. **Fix shape (not yet built):** a release must be a single act that either ships both stores or fails loudly. Options in preference order — (1) one `scripts/release.sh` that bumps ONCE and drives both store scripts with `--no-bump`, so the version can only advance when both uploads are attempted, which is how `+58` was in fact shipped by hand today; (2) a parity check that queries `google_play_track_version_codes` and the App Store Connect API for the latest build on each and fails when they differ, runnable standalone so drift is detectable without a release; (3) at minimum, a loud warning in each single-store script that it is advancing a version the other store will not receive. **The guard is the part that matters** and must not be a comment in a runbook: a check that runs, since the whole failure mode here is that a silent skip looks identical to a successful release. **`--no-commit` remains mandatory on `build_testflight.sh`** whenever it is invoked (its `--commit` path does a bare `git commit`, which sweeps a concurrent track's staged work — a separate known trap, not this defect). Relates to **CR040** (degrade loudly — the skip is invisible by construction), **CR048** (which introduced the Play path as a second, parallel pipeline), **`failure_patterns.md` P11** (one rule, N call sites), and the **promotion protocol**, which governs backend rsync to Alpha and says nothing about store parity. | open | — | AT:R65 |

Candidate guards: a session-scoped check that fails loudly if any test constructs a staleness-sensitive provider without an explicit `now`, or a CI job that runs the suite with a clock advanced 30/90 days so expiries surface before they bite.
